stages.name: Shut-down points
stages.title: Shut-down points
stages.sub: Work out when a loss-making firm should stay open, and when it should close down.

steps.q: A firm is at its profit-maximising output. Its average revenue is £8 and average total cost is £10. Is it making a profit or a loss, and how big is the gap per unit?
steps.hint: Compare revenue per unit to cost per unit at that output.

steps.q: Even if it shuts down completely and produces nothing, a firm still has to pay its rent and loan repayments. Do these costs disappear if output is zero?
steps.wrong: Yes, they also fall to zero
steps.hint: Rent and loan repayments do not depend on how much is produced.

steps.q: A firm is making a loss. Its average revenue covers its average variable cost and leaves a bit over towards rent, but not all of it. Is it better off producing, or producing nothing at all?
steps.hint: If it shuts down it pays all its fixed costs anyway and earns nothing towards them. If it produces, does it get some money towards those fixed costs?

steps.q: Now imagine revenue does not even cover the variable costs of making each unit. Every extra unit made loses money beyond what fixed costs already cost. Should the firm carry on producing?
steps.hint: If each unit adds to the loss on top of fixed costs, does producing more help or make things worse?

steps.q: A firm's revenue covers all its variable costs and some, but not all, of its fixed costs, quarter after quarter with no sign of improving. Is this a situation it can keep going forever?
steps.wrong: Yes, it can carry on forever
steps.hint: Covering variable costs keeps it open today, but what happens to unpaid fixed costs over time?

steps.q: On a diagram, a firm's AR sits below its ATC curve at every output, permanently, with no prospect of AR ever rising above ATC. What does this whole picture show about the firm's future?
steps.right: It will exit in the long run
steps.wrong: It will stay open long run
steps.hint: This is about total cost, not just variable cost, and about the long run, not just today.
